label: Relief and development programmes abroad: shared figures (ours)

rows.label: Treatment of severe acute malnutrition: share of the deaths among untreated children it averts
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 60% (40-80%): children treated in community programmes for severe acute malnutrition die at about 3-5%, against about 10% untreated. Read by the multi-sector relief models' nutrition branches, against their own untreated death rate.

rows.label: Livelihood programmes abroad: cost per household reached (US$)
rows.explainer: Our judgment, $200 ($80-500): savings groups cost about $20-40 a member, livelihood packages with assets and training several hundred dollars a household, graduation programmes more (Banerjee et al. 2015). Read by the multi-sector relief models whose livelihood work publishes spending but not households reached.

rows.label: Livelihood programmes abroad: consumption gain per household reached, share of consumption

source.title: Steinert, Zenker, Filipiak, Movsisyan, Cluver and Shenderovich (2018), Do saving promotion interventions increase household savings, consumption, and investments in Sub-Saharan Africa? A systematic review and meta-analysis, World Development 104:238-256, doi:10.1016/j.worlddev.2017.11.018
source.note: Pooled intention-to-treat effect on household expenditure and income 0.066 SD (SE 0.02, 11 studies); the meta-regression finds smaller consumption effects for longer-cycle programmes (0.10 - 0.05 = 0.05 SD) and mainly female participants (0.09 - 0.06 = 0.03 SD), as savings groups are. Per-capita consumption's SD is about its mean in these samples (35.5 against 35.7 in the three-country trial's control group, Karlan et al. 2017, PNAS, Table 1), so 0.03 SD is about 3% of consumption per household offered.

rows.explainer: Our judgment, 3% (0.5-8%): the meta-analysis of savings-promotion trials in sub-Saharan Africa finds a small gain (about 0.03-0.07 SD, Steinert et al. 2018); graduation programmes, which cost far more a household, raise consumption about 5-10% (Banerjee et al. 2015). Read with @relief_development.livelihood_cost_per_household.

rows.label: Livelihood programmes abroad: years the gain lasts
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 2 years (1-4): the savings-promotion trials in sub-Saharan Africa measured gains 2-3 years after groups began, and their meta-analysis finds effects smaller at later follow-ups (Steinert et al. 2018, World Development, Table 5); groups often keep meeting and assets and skills keep part of a gain, but most programme gains fade without support. The high end allows for work that keeps paying longer (restored rangelands, drought-tolerant farming). Read by every model of ours with a livelihood branch abroad.

rows.label: Relief and development work: years from spending to the benefit
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 0.3 years (0.1-0.8) for a charity whose spending mixes emergency relief with development work: cash, food and water reach people in weeks (the low end), while health, livelihood, savings-group and schooling work takes months to start paying (the high end, close to a year).

rows.label: Health programmes abroad: illness averted beside the deaths, as a share of the deaths' value
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 10% (0-30%): wasting, stunting, maternal illness and newborn complications averted and fewer sick days, beside the deaths. GiveWell's supplementary adjustments for child-health programmes run about 5-20%; for maternal and newborn care the Cochrane review of community packages also finds maternal illness down about a quarter. Read by the multi-sector models' child, maternal and newborn health branches.
